strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated gradient-free bi-objective (stretch-and-squeeze) framework that unifies invariance discovery and adversarial attack generation under a common formalism, addressing a real gap between MEI-based feature visualization and invariance characterization.

Comprehensive experimental validation: pixel-space distance analyses, SVC discriminability of invariant image classes across layers, representational distance analysis across the network hierarchy, and human/observer-network psychophysics, all converging on a coherent hierarchical story (luminance/contrast at low levels, texture at mid levels, pose/viewpoint at high levels).

Interesting and non-trivial comparative finding between robust and standard networks (robust network invariant images are more human/CNN recognizable, with opposing depth-dependent trends), which connects to and extends prior metamer literature (Feather et al.) in a meaningful way.

Reasonably strong human-subject psychophysics methodology (pre-registered-style screening, GLMM with FDR correction, comparison to multiple observer CNNs) and thoughtful robustness checks (subsampling of representational space) relevant to potential neuroscience applications.

Method is model-agnostic and demonstrated to work with hidden-layer targets and heavily subsampled representations, suggesting practical applicability to real neurophysiology experiments with limited recording capacity.
Code and data availability stated (open-source), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single subject architecture (ResNet-50, standard vs. one L2-robust variant); no experiments on other architectures (e.g., ViTs, other CNN families) despite the paper's claims of general applicability, weakening claims about generality of the hierarchical invariance findings.

The optimization convergence statistics (Supplementary A.3) show that many invariance searches at mid/high levels did not converge (e.g., only 5.84%-32.60% converged for standard network high_level/mid_level), raising concerns about how much of the reported qualitative/quantitative trends are influenced by non-converged runs, though the authors argue final populations still reach functionally relevant activation regimes.

The generative prior (a fixed pretrained deep generator, fc7-based) inherently constrains and biases the space of "invariant" images that can be discovered, which is somewhat in tension with the claim of an "unbiased" framework; this limitation is not deeply discussed.

No direct in vivo/biological neural data is used; all "neuroscience applicability" claims rest on simulated subsampling of artificial network units, so the paper's translational claims to biological visual systems remain speculative until validated experimentally (acknowledged as future work, but this tempers the significance claims in the abstract/discussion).

Quantitative effect sizes for some key claims (e.g., correlation of human vs. observer-network accuracy patterns in Fig. 5d) are described qualitatively ("highly correlated") without always reporting explicit correlation coefficients or statistical tests in the main text.
The paper's discussion of why larger/higher-performing standard networks show different recognizability trends is somewhat speculative and not further tested with additional experiments or controls.

Only one robust-training configuration (L2, eps=3) is tested; robustness findings might not generalize across different robust training recipes (L_inf, different epsilon values, different architectures) since the choice of ε or norm type could significantly change invariance geometry.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel, well-motivated gradient-free framework (SnS) that unifies invariance and adversarial-vulnerability probing within a single bi-objective (Pareto) optimization, addressing a real gap left by gradient-based metamer/MEI approaches that require differentiable models.

Extensive and carefully designed experimental validation: quantitative pixel-distance and representational-distance analyses, PCA/SVC layer-discriminability tests, intrinsic dimensionality estimation (PCA and 2NN-ID), convergence diagnostics, and single-loss ablations that convincingly demonstrate the necessity of the dual stretch/squeeze objective.

Strong generalizability demonstration across architectures (ResNet50/18, VGG16, Wide-ResNet, DenseNet, ShuffleNet, ViT, CLIP-ViT) and robustness regimes (L2 and L∞ adversarial training), plus robustness to representation subsampling, directly supporting the claimed applicability to neuroscience settings with sparse recordings.

Human psychophysics experiment (n=25, well-powered 12-AFC task with proper GLMM/Wald chi-square statistics and multiple-comparison correction) combined with multiple observer CNNs yields a novel and interesting empirical finding: L2-robust networks lose interpretability advantage at deep layers, diverging from the standard narrative that robustification uniformly improves human alignment.

Thorough, well-organized supplementary material (34 pages) that substantially strengthens the paper's scientific rigor, including comparisons to metamers, computational resource/reproducibility details, and pseudocode.
weaknesses: The method's expressivity and 'unbiased' invariance discovery are fundamentally bounded by the chosen fc7-based image generator (Dosovitskiy & Brox), which imposes its own prior on the image manifold; this caveat is acknowledged only briefly in the limitations and could substantially shape the reported qualitative/quantitative trends (e.g., lack of high-frequency textures, smoothness of invariant images).

The central neuroscience motivation (applicability to biological recordings) is validated only through subsampling simulations on CNN units, not through any actual biological or in vivo data, so claims of neuroscience readiness remain speculative.

Some interpretive claims (e.g., that SnS 'discovers the actual image variation axes' rather than axes constrained by the generator, or characterizations of qualitative invariance types as luminance/texture/pose) rely on informal visual/qualitative description and could benefit from more rigorous, generator-independent verification.

The comparison between robust and standard network interpretability trends, while striking, is demonstrated primarily on a single generator and largely on ResNet50 variants for the main narrative (with only partial ViT/L∞ extensions in the appendix); the core mechanistic explanation for why L2 robustness fails to help in deep layers is not deeply investigated beyond the empirical observation.

Reproducibility text mentions code and data availability links that appear redacted/incomplete in the provided version, and hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., CMA-ES population size, generator choice, early-stopping thresholds) is not extensively explored.
